results.title: Perfect numbers are the $2$-perfect numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A natural number $n$ is $2$-perfect if and only if it is perfect, that is, $n > 0$ and the sum of the proper divisors of $n$ equals $n$.

results.title: Two Pillai equations in powers of two and three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the integer equation $2^a - 3^b = -1$ holds if and only if $(a, b) = (1, 1)$ or $(a, b) = (3, 2)$. For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$, the integer equation $2^a - 3^b = 2^c - 1$ holds if and only if $(a, b, c) = (2, 1, 1)$, or $(a, b, c) = (4, 2, 3)$, or $b = 0$ and $c = a$.

results.title: Steuerwald's theorem on 3-perfect numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$, $a$, $b$ and $m$ be natural numbers with $N = 2^a 3^b m$, $a \ge 1$, $b \ge 1$, and $m$ coprime to $6$. If $\sigma(N) = 3N$, where $\sigma(N)$ is the sum of the divisors of $N$, then either $a = 1$ and $b \ne 1$, or $a \ne 1$ and $b = 1$.

results.title: Instances of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is a pair $(q, C)$ of a natural number $q$ and a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers. The intended universe is $\{0, \dots, 3q - 1\}$ and the entries of $C$ are the candidate three-element subsets; that each entry lists three distinct elements of the universe is required by well-formedness, not by the type of instances.

results.title: Well-formed EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(q, C)$ of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is well formed when every entry of $C$ is a list of exactly three pairwise distinct natural numbers, each less than $3q$.

results.title: Feasible EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(q, C)$ of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is feasible when $C$ has a sublist $S$, obtained by deleting some entries of $C$, such that for every natural number $x < 3q$ there is exactly one list that occurs in $S$ and contains $x$.

results.title: EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of lists of natural numbers, to an instance of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

results.title: EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Largest infinitely occurring value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$ if $p_k = n$ for infinitely many $k$, and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $p_k = m$ for infinitely many $k$ satisfies $m \le n$.

results.title: Even max-parity condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers (priorities) satisfies the even max-parity condition if there is an even $n$ that is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

results.title: Odd max-parity condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers (priorities) satisfies the odd max-parity condition if there is an odd $n$ that is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

results.title: Bounded sequences have a largest infinitely occurring value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then some natural number $n \le d$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

results.title: The tail of a bounded sequence is bounded by its largest infinitely occurring value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, and let $n$ be the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$. Then $p_k \le n$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

results.title: For bounded sequences the odd parity condition is the negation of the even one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then it satisfies the odd max-parity condition if and only if it does not satisfy the even max-parity condition.

results.title: Max-parity with priorities 1 and 2 is the Büchi condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \in \{1, 2\}$ for every $k$. Then $(p_k)$ satisfies the even max-parity condition if and only if $p_k = 2$ for infinitely many $k$.

results.title: Prefix independence of the largest infinitely occurring value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers and let $j, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in the shifted sequence $(p_{j+k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A sentinel-free word `P` is a prefix of `u ++ ⊥ :: v` (letters lifted to `WithBot α`) exactly when it is a prefix of `u`: the sentinel `⊥` stops every match.

results.title: Rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted: the rotations listed by `sortedRotations t` are in lexicographically nondecreasing order.

results.title: The LF-mapping property
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every row `r`, row `lf (bwt t) r` holds the rotation of row `r` rotated right by one position, i.e. starting one position earlier in the text.

results.title: Inversion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Burrows–Wheeler transform is inverted by the LF-mapping walk.

results.title: FM-index backward search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: FM-index backward search: the half-open row interval `[sp, ep)` for a pattern, computed from the last column alone, processing the pattern from its last letter to its first. The interval for the suffix and `C[c]` are each computed once per letter, so a pattern of length `m` makes `m` recursive calls.

results.title: Backward search returns a genuine row interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Backward search always returns a genuine interval of rows, `sp ≤ ep ≤ |L|`, on any list `L` (so the difference in `backwardSearch_count` involves no truncated subtraction).

results.title: Backward search is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: After processing `P`, the interval `[sp, ep)` is exactly the set of rows whose rotation starts with `P`.

results.title: Counting occurrences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `ep - sp` is the number of positions `i ≤ |t|` at which `P` occurs in `t`.

results.title: Rotations of `t$` compare as suffixes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `i, j ≤ |t|`, rotation `i` of `withSentinel t` is smaller than rotation `j` exactly when suffix `i` is smaller than suffix `j`.

results.title: The Burrows–Wheeler matrix is the suffix array of `t$`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Sorting the rotations of `withSentinel t` orders the starting positions exactly as sorting its suffixes.

results.title: The transform from the suffix array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `bwt[r] = t$[SA[r] - 1]`, the letter cyclically before the suffix of row `r` (the sentinel for the row of the whole text, `SA[r] = 0`).

results.title: Backward-search intervals are suffix-array intervals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Row `r ≤ |t|` lies in the interval `[sp, ep)` computed by backward search on `bwt t` exactly when `P` is a prefix of the suffix of `t` at position `SA[r]`.

results.title: Occurrences of a pattern reported by the FM-index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The occurrences of `P` reported by the FM-index: the suffix-array entries `SA[sp], …, SA[ep - 1]` of the backward-search interval. The BWT and the interval are bound once with `let` and reused, so one query builds the BWT and runs the backward search once, not three times.

results.title: The reported positions are exactly the occurrences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `i` is reported for `P` exactly when `i ≤ |t|` and `P` is a prefix of `t.drop i` (the empty pattern occurs at all `|t| + 1` positions).

results.title: FM-index reports each occurrence once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Each occurrence is reported once.

results.title: Number of FM-index occurrences equals the interval length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The number of reported positions is the length `ep - sp` of the backward-search interval.

results.title: LF in suffix-array terms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a row `r ≤ |t|`, `LF r` is a row and `SA[LF r] = SA[r] - 1` cyclically (`SA[LF r] = |t|` when `SA[r] = 0`).

results.title: The LF step moves one position left in the text
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `SA[r] = SA[LF r] + 1` when `SA[r] > 0`.

results.title: Step-bounded sampled-suffix-array locate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `k` steps of sampled-suffix-array locate from row `r`: return the stored value of the first sampled row reached along the LF-mapping, plus the number of LF steps taken. `sample r` is the stored value `SA[r]` of row `r`, if any.

results.title: Sampled-suffix-array locate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Sampled-suffix-array locate (Ferragina and Manzini 2000): the text position of row `r` from the last column `L` and the samples, with at most `|L|` LF steps.

results.title: Number of LF steps taken by sampled locate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of LF steps `locateAux L sample k r` takes.

results.title: Sampled-suffix-array locate is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every stored value is correct (`sample r = some v → v = SA[r]` for rows `r ≤ |t|`) and every row of text position `0` is sampled, then `locate` returns `SA[r]` for every row `r ≤ |t|`.

results.title: Locate takes at most `s - 1` steps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `0 < s`, if every row whose text position is a multiple of `s` is sampled, then from row `r ≤ |t|` locate makes at most `SA[r] mod s` LF steps (for any amount of fuel `k`). At `s = 0` the `s - 1` bound would be `0` while the proof only gives `SA[r] mod 0 = SA[r]` steps.

part.title: Fitting admixture graphs by least squares

path: Fitting admixture graphs by least squares

results.title: Generalized least-squares qpGraph score S1
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The qpGraph score `S1(g) = -½ (g - f)ᵀ Q⁻¹ (g - f)` (Patterson et al. 2012, eq. 6) of predicted statistics `g` against estimated statistics `f` with error covariance `Q`.

results.title: Least-squares qpGraph score S2
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The least-squares qpGraph score `S2(g) = -∑ᵢ (gᵢ - fᵢ)² / (Qᵢᵢ + λ)` (Patterson et al. 2012, eq. 7). A term with `Qᵢᵢ + λ = 0` is `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.

results.title: Basis independence of the qpGraph score S1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `S1` is basis independent: under an invertible change of basis `A` of the statistics, with the covariance transformed to `A Q Aᵀ`, the score is unchanged. (The identity holds for every `Q`; for singular `Q` both sides are `0` by Mathlib's convention `Q⁻¹ = 0`.)

results.title: The qpGraph score S2 depends on the basis
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `S2` is not basis independent (Patterson et al. 2012, after eq. 7): there are a positive definite covariance `Q`, an invertible change of basis `A` and statistics `f`, `g` such that, for every `λ`, the score changes.

results.title: Score S2 as score S1 with a diagonal covariance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `S2` is twice `S1` with the covariance replaced by the diagonal matrix of the `Qᵢᵢ + λ`, when these are nonzero.

results.title: qpGraph design matrix of basis f4 statistics
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The qpGraph design matrix of basis statistics `f4 (A i) (B i) (C i) (D i)` for lineage weights `w`: entry `(i, e)` is `(w Aᵢ e - w Bᵢ e) * (w Cᵢ e - w Dᵢ e)`.

results.title: Predicted f4 statistics are linear in the edge lengths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the drift model, with the admixture weights fixed, the predicted statistics are linear in the edge lengths: `g = B ℓ` for the design matrix `B`.

results.title: Solutions of the normal equations maximize the score S1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: GLS maximizes `S1`: for positive definite `Q`, a solution `ℓ̂` of the normal equations `Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B ℓ̂ = Bᵀ Q⁻¹ f` maximizes `ℓ ↦ S1(B ℓ)` over all `ℓ`.

results.title: Uniqueness of the generalized least-squares maximizer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Uniqueness of the GLS maximizer: for positive definite `Q` and a design matrix of full column rank (`B.mulVec` injective), a vector `ℓ` with the same score as a solution `ℓ̂` of the normal equations equals `ℓ̂`.

results.title: Invertibility of the generalized least-squares Gram matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive definite `Q` and a design matrix of full column rank, the GLS Gram matrix `Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B` is invertible.

results.title: Closed-form generalized least-squares estimate of edge lengths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The closed-form GLS estimate `ℓ̂ = (Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B)⁻¹ Bᵀ Q⁻¹ f` solves the normal equations when the Gram matrix is invertible.
